newsitem.title: USA: Dollar mostly higher despite exporter complaints. [CORRECTED 00:24 GMT 20/11]
newsitem.headline: Dollar mostly higher despite exporter complaints. [CORRECTED 00:24 GMT 20/11]

text.p: The dollar fell against a strengthening British pound but rose against the German mark and Japanese yen despite new complaints from U.S. businesses that a strong U.S. currency will hurt the economy.

The pound's continued advance against the mark and dollar was the day's highlight, amid expectations that British interest rates will rise further, making sterling-based investments even more attractive.

"Other than that it's been kind of a quiet day. There have been some bearish (dollar) comments that really had no effect on the dollar," said Mark Remigio, a vice president at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, in New York.

Jerry Jasinowski, head of the National Association of Manufacturers, said on Tuesday he expected the Clinton administration to tone down its support for a strong dollar as economic growth slows in 1997. His remarks echoed protests earlier this year by several major U.S. manufacturers.
"The current level of the dollar is preventing the expected boom in U.S. exports from occurring," Jasinowski said. A strong dollar makes U.S. products costlier overseas.
The dollar rose to 111.65 yen from 111.53 yen late Monday and climbed to 1.5055 marks from 1.5020 marks.
The pound rose to a fresh four-year high of $1.6769 on Tuesday and set a 30-month high against the mark. It fetched $1.6755 in late trading, up from $1.6710 late Monday.
Investors have been flocking to the pound since the British government made U.K. investments more attractive by increasing interest rates last month.
Upcoming data is expected to show the U.K. economy remains robust, while persistant signs of inflationary pressures are keeping hopes for another Bank of England rate hike alive, traders said.

"Same story -- people think you are going to see a rate hike potentially at the (Dec. 13) (corrects from "September") monetary meeting," said Anne Pankowski, a vice president at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, in New York. "There is no reason for the trend in sterling to have stalled out yet."
For the second day, the dollar dipped below 1.50 marks in Europe, in part due to reported investor demand for the German currency on the initial stock offering of Deutsche Telekom AG.
Demand from investors around the world outstripped available shares by a huge margin even though the German telecommunications giant decided last week to up its offering by 213 million shares.
"I tend to think now that the share flotation is out of the way, maybe you are going to alleviate some of the selling pressure on (the dollar against the mark)," Pankowski said.

Mark buying petered out in U.S. trading and the dollar got a late day lift after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, an advocate of a stronger dollar, signalled he would keep his job in the second Clinton administration.

Rubin continues to state the administration's support for a strong dollar saying it is in the United States' interest. Despite frequent complaints by exporters, he has rejected suggestions that Washington use the currency as a trade tool.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2715 Swiss francs from 1.2695 Swiss on Monday. It fell to Canadian $1.3419 from C$1.3428.
